2026-08-28|ls-poa-rules: 🎓 Power of Attorney for land: rules, risks, and what holds up in court Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Power of Attorney for Land: Rules, Risks, and What Actually Holds Up in Court — 1acre.in Key Highlights A PoA authorises someone to ACT for you — sign, register, manage, negotiate. It can never hand over ownership. Suraj Lamp (Supreme Court, 2011) settled it: a PoA is not a title-transfer instrument; Shakeel Ahmed (2023) confirmed old GPA chains get no pass. A PoA normally DIES with the principal (Section 201) — except where the agent holds a real interest in the property (Section 202). Registration is mandatory whenever a PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer. Stamp duty turns on the relationship: close family pay nominal rates; unrelated buyers/developers face conveyance-level charges. What a PoA actually does for land One person — the principal — authorises another — the agent — to act on their behalf: signing agreements, handling Sub-Registrar paperwork, managing tenants, negotiating a sale. Representative authority only. The persistent confusion is treating a PoA as a stand-in for a sale — it is not and cannot be: under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, only a REGISTERED SALE DEED transfers title to immovable property. GPA vs SPA: picking the instrument A General PoA grants sweeping authority — suited to an NRI overseeing property across years and distance, but broad authority is hard to police, and if the agent oversteps, the very breadth makes the overstep harder to prove. A Special PoA is built for ONE job and expires when it is done. For land, advocates lean SPA: narrow scope, less room for misuse, cleaner record. What the Supreme Court has said Suraj Lamp (2011) : the “GPA sale” — the once-common practice of selling property via GPA + agreement + will, skipping the sale deed and its stamp duty — transfers NO title. Shakeel Ahmed (2023) : confirmed the principle applies to old chains too — decades-old GPA transactions do not ripen into ownership with time. If your seller’s ownership story runs through a GPA instead of a registered deed, there is no ownership in the story. Example: A Shamshabad plot is offered cheap: the “owner” bought it in 2008 “on GPA” from the recorded owner and has possession ever since. Under Suraj Lamp he owns nothing — only the recorded owner (or their heirs) can convey. The fix, if everyone is alive and willing: a proper registered sale deed from the true owner now, with duty paid. Without that, the plot is unbuyable at any discount. The five classic PoA risks 1) Revoked but presented as valid — an unregistered cancellation shows no outward sign, so a revoked PoA can still deceive a third party. 2) Death of the principal — agency ends automatically under Section 201; anything signed after is void — except the narrow Section 202 case where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property itself. 3) Tangled chains of sub-authority — each PoA granting power to the next makes true ownership harder to trace; buyers inherit disputes they never saw. 4) Self-dealing — an agent selling to HIMSELF is valid only if the PoA explicitly permits it; otherwise a breach of fiduciary duty. 5) Missing registration — where a PoA permits sale, gift or transfer, registration at the sub-registrar is not optional; skipping it guts the document’s standing. Definition — Section 202 (Contract Act): the exception that makes a PoA survive the principal’s death: when the agent has a real INTEREST in the property (say, money already advanced against it), the authority is coupled with that interest and does not lapse. Everything else dies with the principal. Registration, stamp duty, validity Registration is mandatory when the PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer; a PoA limited to rent collection follows lighter rules. Stamp duty follows the relationship : close family typically nominal; an unrelated buyer or developer holding a sale-empowering PoA can face conveyance-level duty — precisely to kill the GPA-sale dodge. NRIs : execute before the Indian mission (or apostille in Hague-convention countries) and stamp within three months of the document reaching India. How to verify a land PoA before acting on it ☐ The PoA names the exact survey number, the exact act, and a duration. ☐ Registered, where the sale/irrevocable/interest test applies. ☐ A revocation clause built in from day one. ☐ The principal INDEPENDENTLY confirmed as owner — in the state land record, not the PoA’s own recitals. ☐ The principal confirmed ALIVE (for a Section 201 document, this is not a formality). ☐ EC pulled — showing any PoA, mortgage or transaction already registered against the parcel. ☐ The land itself transferable — no assigned/prohibited/acquisition taint, because no PoA overrides a land-law restriction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a PoA be used to SELL land? An agent under a valid, registered, sale-empowering PoA can EXECUTE a sale deed for the owner — but the PoA itself never makes anyone an owner. Does calling it “irrevocable” make it irrevocable? No — the label doesn’t; only a genuine Section 202 interest does. What if the principal dies? Authority ends; post-death signatures are void (Section 202 excepted). Stamp duty? Relationship-dependent — nominal for close family, conveyance-level for unrelated sale-empowered holders. Bottom line A PoA is a tool for ACTING at a distance, not for owning. Verify the principal, the registration, the scope and the land’s own transferability — and treat any ownership chain that runs through a GPA as a chain with a missing link. For you: Two rules for your desk. Buying: any parcel whose chain contains a “GPA sale” is unpriced risk — either the true owner signs a fresh registered deed or you pass. Structuring your own JDs: the development GPA you take from landowners should be SPECIAL, scoped to the project, registered, with the JDA’s reversion clause mirrored in it — broad GPAs frighten landowners and courts alike. Documents you will need ☐ Title deed and the 30-year chain of title. ☐ Updated land-record extract — registered deed, 7/12, patta, or your state’s equivalent (pattadar passbook in Telangana). ☐ Survey sketch, master plan extract, and an EC. ☐ NOCs from agriculture, town planning, forest or water-resources departments where applicable. Getting the file right the FIRST time saves months of back-and-forth. The step-by-step process 1) Pull the master plan extract; confirm the zone permits residential use. 2) File the application with the revenue or planning authority for your state and zone. 3) Pay the conversion fee — assessed on area, location and proposed use. 4) Site inspection: an official verifies the land matches the application. 5) Receive the conversion order; the land record is updated. 6) READ THE CONDITIONS on pages two and three — they decide whether the order stays alive. 7) Apply for building-plan sanction from the local body before any construction starts — conversion permits the USE; the sanction permits the BUILDING. Common challenges The zone itself blocking the change — no application can convert green-belt, forest or protection-zone land. Delays or rejection from incomplete files, missing NOCs, or mismatches found at inspection. And the quiet one: conversion orders that LAPSE because construction timelines or conditions went unmet — leaving the land agricultural despite a framed approval on the wall. Example: A buyer pays a premium for a “converted” plot with a 2019 order. Condition 4 on page two required construction to commence within three years; nothing was built. The order lapsed in 2022 — the parcel is agricultural again, and the premium bought paper. One reading of the conditions would have repriced the deal. Best practices before you start Master plan zone first; then road access, water and soil. A short consultation with a local surveyor costs less than discovering a blocking issue after the fee is paid. And engage someone who knows THAT district’s revenue office — procedures genuinely differ between neighbouring districts. Quick answers (FAQ) Is conversion mandatory before building a house? Generally yes — building on unconverted agricultural land invites demolition and denies you sanction, loans and clean resale. Who approves? The competent revenue or planning authority (RDO/Collector-side in Telangana, with HMDA/DTCP layers for layouts). Can any land be converted if I pay? No — the zone decides; money cannot move a green belt. Does an order expire? Yes — it is conditional and time-bound; verify validity when buying “converted” land. Can NRIs apply? For land they lawfully hold (e.g. inherited) — subject to the same zoning rules. If I skip conversion? Unauthorised use: penalties, demolition risk, no sanction, and a discount when you sell. Bottom line Conversion is a sequence, not a fee: zone first, statute second, payment last — and the order you receive is a living document with conditions and an expiry. Read it like a contract, because it is one. For you: This is the machinery of your margin: farmland in, NA/DTCP-approved plots out. Your edge is the SEQUENCE discipline — verify the master-plan zone before the land is even priced, and when buying “converted” parcels from others, audit the order’s conditions and dates like a bank would. 2026-08-29|dd-paigah-registration: DEEP DIVE OF THE DAY Telangana just reopened registration on 1,500 frozen Paigah acres — in the same corridor, the same week, a plot next door sold for ₹269 crore an acre Deep Dive of the Day · anchor reporting from Siasat (“Telangana govt to clear the way to legalise disputed Paigah land”) · cross-read against Telangana Today, Deccan Chronicle, The Hans India and The Federal on the wider Section 22A saga, and Wikipedia/PRS-style background on the Paigah estate and Registration Act · direct WebFetch to telanganatoday.com, siasat.com, thehansindia.com and deccanchronicle.com was blocked by this environment’s network policy, so every fact was built by cross-checking independent search results; the 28 August announcement itself surfaced on only one outlet in this research (Siasat) — marked explicitly below wherever this deep dive rests on that single source rather than multiple corroborating reports 1 · The story, explained from zero — fact by fact F1 · What the government announced Telangana Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy said the government will remove CS-14 and CS-7 Paigah lands from the Section 22A prohibited list and allow “conditional registrations” on them. Plain English — Two big blocks of Hyderabad land that have been legally frozen — no one could register a sale on them — are being unfrozen, but with strings attached, not a clean release. Mechanics — Section 22A of the Registration Act is a blacklist: a sub-registrar must refuse to register any document touching a survey number on that list. Taking CS-14 and CS-7 off it restores the sub-registrar’s ability to accept registrations there — but only in the specific “conditional” form the government is prescribing, not as an ordinary clean sale. Incentives — The government gets to be seen fixing the Section 22A mess it has been under fire for all August, without having to actually resolve the underlying 1958 ownership dispute first — it offloads the litigation risk onto the register itself rather than the state exchequer. Numbers — Two survey groups (CS-14, CS-7) covering an estimated 1,500 acres across Ranga Reddy and Medchal-Malkajgiri districts. F2 · What “conditional registration” actually means on paper Registration documents on CS-14/CS-7 land will explicitly state that ownership rights remain subject to the final outcome of pending proceedings before the Supreme Court and the Telangana High Court. Plain English — You can register the sale, but the deed itself will carry a warning label: “this title could still be overturned by a court that hasn’t ruled yet.” Mechanics — A normal registered sale deed is treated as strong, near-final evidence of ownership. A conditional one is a hybrid: registered (so it clears the immediate 22A block, and lets mutation, loans and resale processes restart) but explicitly incomplete as proof of title, because the underlying court cases haven’t been decided. Incentives — For the government, this is the cheapest possible fix: it unlocks transactions (and the registration revenue that comes with them) today, while leaving the actual legal risk sitting with whoever buys or refinances the property tomorrow. Numbers — No official conditional-registration format has been published yet as of 28 August; the government says instructions will follow case by case. F3 · The scale: thousands of existing homes, several of Hyderabad’s hottest micro-markets The move could regularise thousands of existing constructions — apartments, gated communities — that have come up over decades on CS-14/CS-7 land in Hafeezpet, Kondapur, Hydernagar, Hasmatpet, Malkajgiri and Miyapur, plus Raidurg. Plain English — This isn’t empty farmland. It is finished apartment towers and gated communities where people already live — who, until now, could not cleanly sell, mortgage or will their own homes because the underlying survey numbers sat on a prohibited list. Mechanics — Construction on disputed land does not wait for litigation to finish; builders built, buyers bought, and the paperwork gap only bites years later, exactly when an owner tries to sell, inherit, or borrow against the flat. Incentives — Every one of these named micro-markets is a corridor where plotting and JD activity is already dense — which is exactly why this fix matters more to a developer than an ordinary 22A story about a handful of stray survey numbers. Numbers — Six to seven named localities; “thousands” of constructions, no official count yet published. F4 · Where the dispute comes from: two Paigah estates, one 1958 lawsuit CS-14 land traces to the estate of Nawab Khursheed Jah Paigah, covering Hydernagar, Hasmatpet, Malkajgiri and Hafeezpet; CS-7 land traces to the estate of Asman Jah Paigah, covering Miyapur and Raidurg. Both disputes stem from Civil Suits filed in 1958. Plain English — The Paigahs were a noble family under the old Hyderabad State, second only to the Nizam in rank, who held huge private estates before independence. When those estates passed down, through inheritance, sale and eventual government claims, ownership was contested in court — and that court fight is, remarkably, still not fully settled 68 years later. Mechanics — A Civil Suit (CS) number is how Indian courts track a specific lawsuit; “CS-14 of 1958” and “CS-7 of 1958” are two separate original suits whose outcomes still govern who legally owns these two estate blocks today. Incentives — Sixty-eight years of litigation is not an accident of slow courts alone — large, valuable estates with multiple competing claimants (heirs, buyers, the government itself) tend to generate appeal after appeal precisely because every side has a lot to lose by giving up. Numbers — 68 years between the original 1958 suits and this 2026 partial administrative fix. F5 · A 2009 memo already tried to fix part of this — and the fix itself later got frozen A memo issued in May 2009 directed mutation in favour of decree holders and their registered assignees over CS-14 lands; after that, the same lands were placed under Section 22A, blocking registrations. In survey numbers 77 to 80 of Hafeezpet village, court decrees have been confirmed up to the Supreme Court, yet the land remains under prohibition even though only about 50 acres in survey no. 80 remain vacant. Plain English — The government already tried once, seventeen years ago, to let winners of the court case update the land records in their name. Then, separately, revenue officials froze the same land anyway under the 22A prohibited list — even in survey numbers where the Supreme Court itself has already confirmed who owns what. Mechanics — This is the same structural failure the wider Section 22A crisis has exposed all August: the prohibited list is applied by survey number, mechanically, without checking whether a specific parcel already has a final, even Supreme-Court-level, resolution. Incentives — It shows the 2026 “conditional registration” fix is not solving a fresh problem — it is undoing a bureaucratic freeze the state’s own earlier order should have prevented, which is part of why critics call the 22A rollout sloppy rather than deliberate. Numbers — Survey nos. 77–80, Hafeezpet village; ~50 acres in survey no. 80 alone remain vacant, undeveloped land inside an otherwise built-up, Supreme-Court-confirmed block. F6 · The revenue angle: roughly ₹1,000 crore the state has been unable to collect Unlocking CS-14/CS-7 registrations is expected to unlock an estimated ₹1,000 crore in registration revenue for the state. Plain English — Every blocked registration is stamp duty and registration-fee income the government cannot collect — on a state whose own CAG report this month flagged a widening revenue deficit. Mechanics — Registration and stamp duty are among the fastest, most reliable revenue levers a state government controls directly, unlike tax devolution or central scheme funding, which depend on Delhi’s timetable. Incentives — A cash-squeezed state has every reason to unfreeze a ₹1,000-crore revenue pool quickly, even via an imperfect “conditional” fix, rather than wait years for the Supreme Court and High Court to finish with CS-14 and CS-7. Numbers — ~₹1,000 crore estimated unlocked registration revenue; this is the same month Telangana’s CAG report flagged a ₹19,266.83-crore four-month revenue deficit. F7 · The fix is case-by-case, not a blanket release Revenue Department Principal Secretary D.S. Lokesh Kumar said instructions on CS-14/CS-7 lands would be issued case by case, factoring in the various court judgments relating to specific properties. Plain English — This is not a single switch flipped for all 1,500 acres at once — every parcel will still need its own individual clearance, checked against whatever that specific piece of litigation has decided so far. Mechanics — Different portions of CS-14 and CS-7 sit at different stages of litigation — some have High Court decrees, some have Supreme Court confirmation (like survey nos. 77–80 above), some are still actively contested — so a blanket rule would either wrongly free contested land or wrongly keep settled land frozen. Incentives — Case-by-case processing protects the government legally (it isn’t pre-judging any pending case) but also means the practical relief for any individual owner depends entirely on how fast and how fairly the Revenue Department works through each file — the exact kind of discretionary, file-by-file process that has fuelled complaints (and an alleged “30% commission” racket, per earlier August reporting) throughout the wider Section 22A saga. Numbers — No published timeline or queue order for how the case-by-case clearances will be sequenced. F8 · The Raidurg connection: the same corridor is being repriced upward the same week CS-7 land explicitly covers Miyapur and Raidurg — the same Knowledge City/Raidurg corridor where TGIIC’s Plot P2 auction fetched a record ₹269 crore per acre this week, the third record broken in this corridor within the year. Plain English — In the exact same stretch of the city, two very different things are happening at once: government-auctioned commercial land is being priced ever higher in public tenders, while nearby residential land trapped by a 68-year-old title dispute is only now becoming legally saleable again. Mechanics — These are legally unconnected processes — one is TGIIC auctioning its own clean-titled industrial land, the other is the Revenue Department unfreezing privately-built residential land under a different law — but they sit inside the same physical corridor, meaning the same underlying demand story (IT-corridor growth, GCC expansion, Knowledge City proximity) is driving both. Incentives — For anyone landbanking or JD-negotiating in Miyapur/Raidurg, this is effectively a double signal: institutional buyers are willing to pay record prices for clean land here, and a fresh supply of previously-frozen residential land is about to become transactable in the same belt — though the second kind carries the conditional-title risk the first kind does not. Numbers — ₹269 crore/acre (Raidurg Plot P2, this week) vs. an unquantified but real supply of newly-registrable, litigation-flagged CS-7 land in the same corridor. F9 · This lands in the middle of a month-long political firestorm over Section 22A Minister Ponguleti has separately had to admit “22A errors” and apologise over the wider prohibited-list controversy this August, after BRS’s Harish Rao demanded a white paper, BJP’s Malkajgiri MP Eatala Rajender called the government’s handling “arbitrary” and “Tughlaq,” and BJP state leaders demanded a judicial probe. Plain English — This isn’t a quiet technical announcement — it is the government trying to show progress on a land-records mess that has become a genuine political liability, with both major opposition parties attacking it from different angles all month. Mechanics — Announcing a concrete fix for one named, high-profile chunk of the 22A problem (Paigah land, ~1,500 acres, a defined revenue number) is easier and more visible than fixing the diffuse, colony-by-colony wrongful listings the opposition has been highlighting elsewhere. Incentives — The government gets a positive headline (“government unlocks 1,500 acres”) that can sit alongside, and partly offset, the negative ones (“government wrongly froze thousands of clean homes”) from the same underlying law. Numbers — The wider 22A relaxation drive has reportedly cleared ~98% of over 300 relaxation applications government-wide, per the Revenue Minister’s own, not yet independently audited, figures from earlier in August. F10 · A single-source caveat, stated plainly Every article found reporting this specific 28 August CS-14/CS-7 conditional-registration announcement traces back to one outlet, Siasat; no second independent news organisation was found to have separately confirmed the announcement within this research. Plain English — The underlying facts — the Paigah dispute, the 1958 suits, the survey numbers, the minister’s name and portfolio — are all independently, historically well documented. But the specific claim that the government made this announcement on 28 August rests on one outlet’s reporting in this research, not a cross-confirmed multi-source story. Mechanics — This is exactly the kind of gap this edition’s sourcing method is built to surface rather than paper over: where a fact could not be confirmed twice, it is marked, not silently treated as certain. Incentives — Readers acting on this — especially anyone with property in CS-14/CS-7 survey numbers — should treat “conditional registration is now available” as a strong lead to verify directly with the Sub-Registrar or Revenue Department before relying on it, not as a confirmed, bureaucratically live process yet. Numbers — 1 primary source found for the core announcement; multiple independent sources for all surrounding context. Coverage check: 10 fact-units (F1–F10) covered above — the announcement and its mechanics, the scale and geography, the 1958 origin of the dispute, the 2009 partial fix and its own failure, the revenue motive, the case-by-case caveat, the Raidurg-corridor connection, the political backdrop, and an explicit single-source flag on the core claim. No material fact surfaced in research was left uncovered. 2 · Who’s who and what’s what — the dossiers Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy — Telangana Revenue & Housing Minister What he is: Cabinet minister in charge of the Revenue Department, which administers Section 22A, land records, and now this Paigah-land fix. Backstory — A senior Congress leader from Khammam, Ponguleti has held the Revenue and Housing portfolios through a difficult month: he has spent much of August publicly defending, and at points apologising for, the Section 22A rollout after thousands of property owners found their homes wrongly listed as prohibited. He has repeatedly cited a self-reported clearance figure of roughly 98% of relaxation applications resolved. Why he’s in this story / incentive — As the minister directly answerable for the 22A crisis, announcing a concrete, named fix for one large chunk of it (Paigah land) is politically necessary for him personally, not just administratively useful. Power map — Answers to Chief Minister Revanth Reddy and the state Cabinet; his direct political attackers this month have been BRS’s Harish Rao and BJP’s Eatala Rajender. D.S. Lokesh Kumar — Principal Secretary, Revenue Department What he is: The senior bureaucrat running the Revenue Department’s day-to-day administration under Minister Ponguleti. Backstory — As Principal Secretary, he is the official who translates ministerial announcements like this one into the actual case-by-case instructions Sub-Registrars will follow. Why he’s in this story / incentive — His statement that CS-14/CS-7 relief will be handled “case by case” is the single most important qualifier in the whole announcement — it is the difference between a genuine blanket unlock and a slow, discretionary, file-by-file process. Power map — Reports to the Revenue Minister and the state Chief Secretary; supervises the district-level Revenue and Registration officials who will actually process each conditional registration. The Paigah family — Nawab Khursheed Jah Paigah (CS-14) and Asman Jah Paigah (CS-7) What they were: Hereditary nobility of the former princely state of Hyderabad, ranked just below the Nizam, historically holding vast private estates (the word “Paigah” itself denotes their rank and estate system). Backstory — The Paigah nobles built palaces, mosques and endowments across old Hyderabad and held large agricultural and urban landholdings that, after Indian independence and the integration of Hyderabad State in 1948, became subject to inheritance disputes, government claims and eventual litigation as the city expanded over what had been their rural estate land. Why they’re in this story / incentive — Their historical estates are the literal ground beneath CS-14 and CS-7 — the family (or, more precisely, their heirs, decree holders and assignees) are among the private claimants in the 1958 suits still being litigated today. Power map — No formal power today; their legal successors (heirs, and parties who purchased decree rights) are private litigants against the state and against each other in the pending Supreme Court and High Court cases. Section 22A, Registration Act, 1908 What it is: A Telangana-specific provision empowering the state to maintain a district-wise list of survey numbers — covering government, endowment/waqf, and disputed or ceiling-surplus land — that Sub-Registrars must refuse to register documents against. Backstory — Intended to stop fraudulent sale of government or disputed land, it has instead swept up thousands of legitimate, patta-holding private properties throughout August 2026 because it is applied mechanically by survey number rather than by verified current ownership status. Why it’s in this story / incentive — It is the exact legal mechanism CS-14 and CS-7 are being partially released from — and the same mechanism this whole month’s wider political controversy has centred on. Telangana High Court & Supreme Court of India What they are: The two judicial forums where CS-14 and CS-7’s underlying ownership disputes remain pending, even after 68 years. Backstory — Portions of these suits have already reached final Supreme Court confirmation (as in Hafeezpet survey nos. 77–80), while other portions remain actively contested at various stages — explaining why the government’s fix has to be case-by-case rather than blanket. Why they’re in this story / incentive — Every “conditional” registration issued under this policy is explicitly pegged to whatever these courts eventually decide — making their pending rulings the real, still-unresolved variable behind every transaction made under the new rule. TGIIC — Telangana Industrial Infrastructure Corporation What it is: The state body that auctioned Raidurg Plot P2 for ₹269 crore/acre this week — see today’s Telangana Real Estate zone for the full story. Why it’s in this story / incentive — Not a direct actor in the Paigah announcement, but its record-breaking Raidurg auctions sit in the same CS-7 geography (Miyapur/Raidurg), making it the market-price backdrop against which this land-title unlock should be read. Harish Rao & Eatala Rajender — opposition critics of the 22A rollout What they are: BRS Deputy Floor Leader (Harish Rao) and BJP Malkajgiri MP (Eatala Rajender), the two most vocal opposition critics of the government’s Section 22A handling this August. Why they’re in this story / incentive — Their sustained pressure — Harish Rao’s white-paper demand, Eatala’s “Tughlaq decision” framing — is the direct political cost this announcement is partly designed to offset; both stand to gain politically regardless of whether the government’s fix works, by having forced it into the open. Power map — Both answer to their respective party leaderships (BRS, BJP) and are positioning ahead of the next election cycle on land and governance issues. BIAS NOTE — how this story is being covered This entire deep dive rests overwhelmingly on Siasat’s reporting for the core 28 August announcement, with Telangana Today, Deccan Chronicle and The Hans India providing only the surrounding Section 22A political context (Ponguleti’s apology, Harish Rao and Eatala’s attacks) rather than independent confirmation of the Paigah-specific fix itself. No direct, on-record government statement beyond the minister’s quoted remarks and the Principal Secretary’s case-by-case caveat was found; no property-owner or developer reaction to this specific announcement was found in this research, since it broke very recently. Readers should treat the announcement as credible but not yet fully cross-verified, and should independently confirm with the Sub-Registrar’s office before relying on “conditional registration” being operational for any specific CS-14/CS-7 parcel. 3 · Glossary — every term, simply Section 22A (prohibited list) — a Telangana-specific rule under the Registration Act, 1908 that lets the state list survey numbers a Sub-Registrar must refuse to register documents against. Example: an entire Hafeezpet apartment block sitting on a CS-14 survey number could not be resold or mortgaged while listed, however clean its individual owners’ paperwork looked. Conditional registration — a registration allowed to proceed, but with the deed itself stating the ownership is not final and remains subject to pending litigation. Example: this is what CS-14/CS-7 buyers will now get instead of an ordinary, unqualified sale deed. Civil Suit (CS) number — the case-tracking number Indian courts assign to a specific lawsuit, used ever after to refer to that dispute and everything it covers. Example: “CS-14 of 1958” is shorthand every Hyderabad land lawyer recognises for one specific, still-unresolved Paigah estate dispute. Decree holder — the party a court has ruled in favour of in a given suit, entitled to whatever the court’s decree grants (here, typically a claim to specific land). Example: the 2009 memo tried to let CS-14 decree holders update land records in their own name. Mutation — the process of updating a government land record to reflect a change of ownership, separate from and following registration. Example: even after a conditional registration, a buyer still needs mutation done at the local revenue office to be reflected as the current record holder. Paigah — the hereditary noble rank and associated landed-estate system of certain aristocratic families under the former princely state of Hyderabad, ranked just below the Nizam himself. Example: Hyderabad’s Paigah Palace and several old estates across the city trace back to this system. Encumbrance / title dispute — any claim, court case, mortgage or restriction attached to a property that clouds a buyer’s ability to get clean, undisputed ownership. Example: CS-14/CS-7 land carries a 68-year-old title dispute as its encumbrance, which conditional registration does not remove — it only lets you transact around it. Relaxation / release (22A) — the formal process of removing a specific survey number from the Section 22A prohibited list once its status is verified as clean or resolved. Example: taking CS-14 and CS-7 off the list, as announced here, is a relaxation at the level of an entire estate rather than a single wrongly-listed plot. Sub-Registrar — the local government office where property documents are actually registered; it is legally barred from registering anything touching a Section 22A-listed survey number. Example: it is the Sub-Registrar’s counter where a CS-14 owner will discover, in practice, whether “conditional registration” is actually available yet for their specific plot. Revenue deficit — a government spending more on day-to-day running costs than it collects in regular income, with no asset created either side. Example: Telangana’s CAG report flagged a ₹19,266.83-crore four-month revenue deficit this August — the same fiscal pressure this ₹1,000-crore registration-revenue unlock is meant to ease. 4 · The backstory — how we got here When What happened 1948 Hyderabad State is integrated into India; the old Paigah noble estates begin the long process of passing into private, contested and government hands as the city grows over former estate land. 1958 Civil Suits No. 14 and No. 7 are filed, contesting ownership over the Khursheed Jah Paigah estate (CS-14) and the Asman Jah Paigah estate (CS-7) respectively. Decades, 1958–2000s As Hyderabad’s western suburbs (Hafeezpet, Kondapur, Miyapur, Raidurg) urbanise rapidly, apartments and gated communities are built across parts of the disputed estate land, even as the underlying court cases continue. May 2009 A government memo directs mutation in favour of CS-14 decree holders and their registered assignees — an early attempt to let court-confirmed owners update land records. After 2009 CS-14 lands are nonetheless placed under Section 22A, freezing registrations again — including, eventually, in survey numbers like 77–80 in Hafeezpet where the Supreme Court itself had already confirmed ownership. Early August 2026 The wider Section 22A crisis breaks into public view: thousands of property owners statewide receive notices that their homes are on the prohibited list; opposition parties demand explanations. Mid-to-late August 2026 Minister Ponguleti admits “22A errors” and apologises; BRS’s Harish Rao demands a white paper; BJP’s Eatala Rajender calls the government’s handling an “arbitrary, Tughlaq decision”; the Revenue Minister cites a self-reported ~98% relaxation-application clearance rate. 17–28 August 2026 In the same weeks, TGIIC runs back-to-back Raidurg land auctions in the CS-7 (Miyapur/Raidurg) corridor, each breaking the previous Hyderabad land-price record — culminating in Plot P2’s ₹269 crore/acre result on 28 August. 28 August 2026 Minister Ponguleti announces CS-14 and CS-7 will be removed from the Section 22A list, with conditional registration allowed pending Supreme Court and High Court outcomes; Principal Secretary D.S. Lokesh Kumar says implementation will be case-by-case. The deeper forces. Two pressures are converging here. First, a records-integrity pressure: Telangana rebuilt its entire land-records system around a new portal (Bhu Bharati, replacing the earlier Dharani) this year, and the government’s own explanation for the wider 22A mess is data-migration error — meaning Paigah land’s specific problem (an old, real litigation risk) got tangled up with a much bigger, newer administrative one (wrongly-listed clean properties), and the fixes for both are now arriving together, in the same news cycle, even though they are different problems with different real risk levels. Second, a fiscal pressure: this state is simultaneously auctioning land at record commercial prices (Raidurg), planning further large-scale monetisation (the 400-acre Gachibowli auction, TGIIC’s roughly ₹15,776-crore debt-repayment obligation), and now unfreezing residential registrations for revenue — three different levers, all pulled toward the same goal of turning Telangana’s land into cash flow while its ordinary revenue collection runs a widening deficit. What a longtime Hyderabad land-watcher knows that a first-time reader does not. Old-estate title disputes like the Paigah suits are not rare curiosities in this city — large chunks of Hyderabad’s western and northern suburbs carry similar inherited-estate or endowment-land shadows, and “we’ll register it conditionally, pending litigation” has precedent as a pragmatic, if imperfect, government tool for keeping a functioning property market alive on land that can never be fully title-cleared quickly. A longtime follower would also recognise this as the second major concession the government has made this month under 22A political pressure (after the minister’s public apology and the ~98% clearance claim) — suggesting the opposition campaign is having real, incremental policy effect, not just noise. 5 · So what — stakes and consequences Who wins. Owners of existing constructions on CS-14/CS-7 land who have been unable to sell, mortgage or transfer their homes for years get a path back to transactability, even if imperfect. The state government gets both a political story (“we fixed part of 22A”) and up to ₹1,000 crore in registration revenue it badly needs given its widening deficit. Developers and plotting professionals active in Hafeezpet, Kondapur, Miyapur and Raidurg gain a fresh, if title-flagged, supply of transactable land and clearer visibility into which parcels are moving from frozen to conditional. Who loses, or carries new risk. Anyone who buys or lends against a conditionally-registered property is explicitly taking on litigation risk the deed itself discloses — if the Supreme Court or High Court eventually rules against the current possessor’s claim, that buyer’s title could unravel, however properly it was registered today. Banks may be reluctant to lend freely against conditional titles until a track record and clearer regulatory framework exists, which could mean this “unlock” helps registration and mutation more than it helps financing in the short term. What happens next — the realistic scenarios. Likely: The Revenue Department issues detailed case-by-case instructions over the coming weeks; early conditional registrations proceed slowly in the most clearly-resolved survey numbers (like Hafeezpet 77–80) while more contested pockets stay frozen pending further clarity. Possible: Banks and NBFCs publicly clarify (or hesitate to clarify) their lending stance on conditionally-registered CS-14/CS-7 properties, which will determine how much real liquidity this unlock actually creates versus how much stays paper-only. Less likely, most consequential: The Supreme Court or High Court issues a fresh, defining ruling on the underlying CS-14/CS-7 suits themselves in the coming months — which would either validate this conditional-registration approach as a reasonable bridge, or expose it as a premature fix that let transactions proceed on land whose true ownership still wasn’t settled. What this means for you. (a) Hyderabad/Telangana real estate: if you have any interest, existing or prospective, in Hafeezpet, Kondapur, Hydernagar, Hasmatpet, Malkajgiri, Miyapur or Raidurg, go find out now whether the specific survey number you care about falls inside CS-14 or CS-7 — this is exactly the kind of change that can quietly reprice a parcel’s liquidity (not its headline value) overnight. Treat any “conditionally registered” property as carrying real, disclosed litigation risk in your underwriting, not as equivalent to a clean title, however tempting the discount. (b) Business/investment generally: a government offering a “conditional” version of a normally-absolute right (here, ownership) is a repeatable pattern worth recognising whenever a state needs to unlock economic activity faster than its courts can resolve the underlying legal question — the label “conditional” is doing a lot of quiet risk-transfer work, and it is worth reading exactly what it makes you responsible for before you rely on it. A beginner reading only the headline would conclude “Telangana just fixed 1,500 acres of land problems.” The sharper read is that the government converted an outright legal block into a disclosed, ongoing risk that individual buyers, lenders and developers must now price in themselves, case by case — a real improvement in liquidity, but not the clean resolution the headline implies. 6 · The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Telangana has spent August 2026 under fire over Section 22A, the land-blacklist rule that wrongly froze thousands of clean properties statewide. 2026-08-29|ls-buy-agri: 🎓 How to buy agricultural land in India: rules, verification, and costs Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Buy Agricultural Land in India: Rules, Verification, and Costs — 1acre.in Key Highlights Eligibility is state law, not national: some states restrict to farmers, others let anyone buy. Ceiling laws cap the total holding — and the cap moves by state and land type. Verification means pulling deed, EC and revenue records YOURSELF — most disputes start in skipped paperwork. The negotiated price is the start of spending: duty, registration, legal and survey fees stack on top. NRIs cannot buy farmland outright — inheritance is their route in. Who can legally buy The land’s state decides, through its land-reform laws. Restricted states demand an agricultural background or eligibility test (with exemption and family routes for some non-farmers); open states — Telangana included — let anyone buy. On top sits the ceiling: a cap on total holdings that varies by state and land type, and crossing it can void the excess. Confirm both BEFORE attachment to a plot sets in. What verification covers, and why The step that decides whether the purchase becomes an asset or a decade of correspondence. The core: title deed — name matches the seller; EC for 15–30 years — loans and claims; latest revenue records — ownership and classification cross-checked (pattadar passbook in Telangana); mutation — actually updated, because an unmutated transfer can be contested later; licensed survey — boundaries on the ground match the paper; encroachment is more common than first-timers expect. The agreement then fixes price, advance and timelines, with the seller’s identity proof and confirmation the land remains agricultural-classified. Example: The skipped-survey classic: 4 acres bought on paper, 3.7 on the ground — the missing 0.3 under a neighbour’s decades-old bund. The survey that would have caught it costs a few thousand rupees; the shortfall cost lakhs and a boundary case. The process in order Eligibility → verification file → agreement (price, advance, timelines) → registered deed at the SRO with duty and fees → mutation so the record names you. Each step gates the next; hurrying the order is how buyers finance other people’s mistakes. The real total cost Beyond the price: stamp duty and registration (state-set — in Telangana around 7.5% all-in on sale deeds), surveyor’s fees, legal consultation, EC charges — several percentage points above the negotiated figure. Planning to build later? Conversion is a separate application, inspection and state-specific fee again. Red flags Ownership disputes and fraud tied to murky chains; government-allotted / assigned land that cannot legally be resold — including land granted to SC/ST families under protective laws, whose restrictions surface only after payment; unchecked mutation; unsurveyed boundaries. The first two are WALK-AWAY flags; the last two are FIX-FIRST flags. Restricted states vs open states Aspect Agriculturist-restricted states Open-purchase states Who may buy Farming background / eligibility tests required Any buyer Legal source State land-reform law State land-reform law Extra friction Exemption applications, proof of background None on eligibility (ceiling still applies) Suits Active farmers Investors and non-farming buyers NRI restrictions A hard line: NRIs and OCIs cannot purchase agricultural land directly under the exchange-control rules; they CAN inherit it. RBI approval exists in theory, rarely in practice, and leans toward genuine agricultural use. (The full NRI story — funding accounts, repatriation caps — is its own class in this school.) Financing reality Banks lend against farmland more cautiously than against houses — expect more cash upfront, slower sanctions, and a lender re-running your whole verification. Use that: a bank’s refusal is free due diligence naming the defect. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Eligibility confirmed for the state. ☐ EC and title deed pulled by YOU. ☐ Latest revenue records compared against the deed for name/classification mismatches. ☐ Mutation status verified. ☐ Licensed survey done before the agreement. ☐ Assigned/restricted-origin ruled out. ☐ Full friction cost (duty + fees) priced into the offer. Quick answers (FAQ) Can anyone buy, or only farmers? Depends on the state — Telangana: anyone; several states: restrictions apply. How far back should the history check go? 30 years standard. Can the land be converted later? If zoning allows — a separate process with its own fee. What are the total costs? Price + roughly 7.5% duty/registration (Telangana) + legal, survey and EC costs. Bottom line Agricultural land rewards patience over speed: eligibility, ceiling, chain, record-match, survey — five checks before money, each cheap, each catching a different disaster. The dispute you avoid was always cheaper than the discount you chased. For you: Make the ritual fixed and identical per parcel: portal check → passbook-vs-deed match → EC 30 years → prohibited-list → chain → survey → THEN price. Ritual beats judgement; it has no optimistic days. And each defect found is either a WALK (assigned taint, water-body extent) or a PRICE (pending mutation, survey shortfall) — knowing which bucket instantly is what “experienced” means. 2026-08-29|ls-dtcp: 🎓 DTCP approval explained: what it means for plot buyers Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: DTCP Approval Explained: What It Means for Plot Buyers — 1acre.in Key Highlights DTCP approval is a LAYOUT permit under state town-planning law — it certifies road width, open-space reservation, zoning and infrastructure. It does NOT certify title. WHICH authority approves depends on where the plot sits — metropolitan areas have their own authorities; DTCP covers the rest. The verification is the LP NUMBER, searched by you on the official portal. A brochure claim is not evidence. A FILE number is not an LP number — “approval in process” means unapproved today. Roads and OSR land inside an approved layout belong to the local body and cannot be sold as plots. What DTCP approval actually certifies A layout permit issued by the Directorate of Town and Country Planning under the state’s town-planning law, confirming the layout meets planning and development standards: road widths, zoning compliance, open spaces, infrastructure provisions. What it never touches: who OWNS the land. An approved layout on a disputed title is still a disputed title with nice roads. Definition — OSR (Open Space Reservation): the share of a layout — typically around 10% — that must be set aside for parks and public purposes and vested in the local body. It is the community’s land; a developer selling “plots” carved from it is selling what is not theirs. DTCP does not apply everywhere The commonest error is checking the right number against the WRONG authority. DTCP’s writ covers the state MINUS the metropolitan planning areas — in Chennai that belt belongs to CMDA; in Hyderabad, HMDA approves inside its boundary while DTCP covers the districts beyond, alongside local and new-town planning authorities issuing equally valid approvals under the same law. First question for any plot: WHOSE jurisdiction is this survey number in? How to verify using the LP number Ask the seller for the approval PROCEEDINGS ORDER and the LP number with its year. Then search it YOURSELF: Telangana — dtcp.telangana.gov.in or the DPMS district-wise approved-layout lists (HMDA’s portal for its belt); Tamil Nadu — onlineppa.tn.gov.in or tcp.tn.gov.in. Older records (roughly ten years plus) often move from the regional office to central storage — an RTI or counter application becomes the route. Then MATCH: survey numbers on the portal against the sale deed; road widths, plot numbers and OSR positions on the approved plan against what is being shown on-site. The plan on the portal is the contract; the site should be its photocopy. Which authority approves what Where the plot sits Approving authority Where to search Metropolitan planning area (e.g. HMDA belt / CMDA) The metropolitan authority Its own approved-layout portal Rest of the state DTCP State DTCP portal / DPMS lists Notified local planning areas Local / new-town planning authority That authority’s records Gram panchayat areas Still the competent planning authority Panchayat “sanction” alone is NOT layout approval The traps that cost buyers money “Approval is in process” — the layout is unapproved TODAY; the number offered is usually a file/application number, and a file number returns nothing on the portal. Gram-panchayat sanction dressed as approval — a panchayat has no power to approve a layout; this is the single most documented fraud pattern in plot sales. OSR and road land sold as plots — reserved areas belong to the local body; corner plots adjoining a reserved zone are where the boundary gets blurred. “Regularisation applied for” — applying under regularisation rules does not make a layout approved; wait for the FINAL order. Approved layout on unconverted land — layout approval and agricultural-land conversion are separate; confirm the conversion order separately. Example: A ₹28-lakh “DTCP-approved” plot near Shadnagar: the brochure prints “LP No. — applied” and a gram-panchayat resolution. Portal search: nothing. Two years later the regularisation application is rejected, the layout stays unapproved, banks refuse loans against every plot in it, and resale prices halve. The five-minute portal search was the whole due diligence. Your checklist before you pay ☐ Confirm which planning authority governs the location. ☐ Get the approval proceedings order + LP number with year. ☐ Search the LP number YOURSELF on the portal; keep the printout. ☐ Match survey numbers, road widths, OSR positions against deed and site. ☐ Treat “in process” and “regularisation applied” as UNAPPROVED. ☐ Run title chain, patta and EC checks separately — approval is not ownership. Quick answers (FAQ) Is approval mandatory before buying? For a safe, financeable, resalable plot — effectively yes. Home loan without it? Banks generally refuse plots in unapproved layouts. Does approval mean clear title? No — planning compliance only. If I buy unapproved anyway? Loan rejection, registration obstacles in some states, regularisation charges if a window opens, demolition exposure if it never does — and a permanent discount at resale. Bottom line One number, one portal, five minutes, your own eyes: the LP-number search is the highest-value check in plot buying. Everything a brochure claims is marketing until the portal agrees. For you: This is YOUR licence to operate — your ventures’ LP numbers are the moat that separates you from the unapproved-layout market. Print the LP number and approved plan into every marketing piece and teach buyers to verify it themselves: the developer who INVITES verification wins the trust war at zero cost.
